glossary.definition: Farming the land by planting crops like wheat and barley and keeping tame animals such as sheep, pigs, and cattle.
A history detective who carefully digs up buried tools, bones, and building remains to discover how ancient people lived.
A tall, bell-shaped clay drinking pot stamped with comb patterns and brought to Britain by newcomers around 2400 BC.
Spotted volcanic boulders hauled 140 miles from the Preseli Hills in Wales to stand inside Stonehenge around 2500 BC.
A tough golden metal made by melting nine parts copper together with one part tin over a hot fire.
The green land bridge that joined Britain to mainland Europe before melting ice flooded the North Sea around 6500 BC.
Wise Iron Age Celtic priests and judges who memorised sacred laws, stories, and prayers instead of writing books.
A circular prehistoric monument framed by a wide dug-out earth ditch set inside a raised outer bank.
A giant Iron Age hilltop settlement ringed by steep earth ramparts, deep ditches, and wooden fences to guard a tribe.
A Stone Age person who moved camp with the seasons to hunt wild animals, catch fish, and pick nuts and berries.
Common reddish rock dug from hills and bogs that blacksmiths heated in clay furnaces to hammer tough iron tools.
Striking hard flint stones carefully to chip off razor-sharp flakes for handaxes, scrapers, and spear tips.
A long earth-and-chalk mound with dark stone chambers inside where Neolithic farming villages buried their ancestors.
The Middle Stone Age from about 10,000 to 4000 BC, when warming forests spread across Britain after the Ice Age.
A hollow two-piece stone shape into which Bronze Age smiths poured glowing liquid metal to cast sharp axe blades.
The New Stone Age from about 4000 to 2500 BC, when Britain's first farmers cleared woods and built year-round villages.
The Old Stone Age from about 850,000 to 10,000 BC, when Ice Age hunters sheltered in caves and chipped flint handaxes.
The huge stretch of human time before anyone in Britain wrote down words, dates, or books.
Two heavy round stones spun with a wooden handle to grind wheat and barley grains quickly into flour.
A circular Bronze or Iron Age family home with woven wattle-and-daub walls, a central hearth fire, and a cone thatched roof.
Massive, rock-hard grey sandstone boulders dragged across Wiltshire on wooden sledges to build Stonehenge's tallest circle.
A curved harvesting tool fitted with a sharp flint blade to slice ripe stalks of wheat and barley.
A 5,000-year-old Neolithic stone village on Orkney in Scotland, uncovered when an 1850 storm blew away coastal sand dunes.
Heating crushed metal-bearing rock in a fierce charcoal fire until shiny liquid metal melts free from the stone.
The longest summer day at Midsummer or shortest winter day at Midwinter, lined up with the stones of Stonehenge.
A heavy, gleaming neck ring twisted from ropes of gold, silver, or bronze and worn by proud Celtic leaders.
A giant three-stone arch at Stonehenge made from two tall upright boulders holding one horizontal lintel stone on top.
Soaked completely full of water and thick mud with no air inside, stopping ancient wood and cloth from rotting away.

concept_widget.title: How Melting Ice Drowned Doggerland and Made Britain an Island
concept_widget.caption: Slide or tap across the three stages to trace how rising meltwater flooded Doggerland around 6500 BC.

stops.label: Before 7000 BC: Walking Across Green Doggerland
stops.summary: Wide grassy valleys, rivers, and marshes joined Britain straight to mainland Europe so Stone Age families walked across on dry land.

traits.value: Low green plains, rivers, and reed marshes linking Britain to Europe.
Families camped beside marshes to spear eels, net ducks, and trap beavers.
Hunters walked dry-footed all the way from mainland Europe into Britain.

stops.label: c. 7000–6500 BC: Melting Ice Pours Into the Sea
stops.summary: As giant northern ice sheets melted, huge amounts of water poured into the sea and crept across low-lying marshes.

traits.value: Rising tides and fierce storms turned low river valleys into salty mudflats.
Hunter-gatherer bands moved camp onto higher hills as hunting grounds flooded.
Dry paths vanished under water and left muddy islands behind.

stops.label: c. 6500 BC: Doggerland Sinks Under the North Sea
stops.summary: Rising waves flooded low Doggerland forever around 6500 BC, cutting Britain off from mainland Europe as an island.

traits.value: Deep North Sea waves covered the old green land bridge forever.
Modern fishing boats still pull mammoth teeth and flint tools from the sea floor.
Every later newcomer to island Britain now had to cross the sea by boat.

concept_widget.title: Three Ages of Prehistoric Tools: Flint, Bronze, and Iron
concept_widget.caption: Tap each tab to compare how prehistoric toolmakers moved from chipped stone to cast bronze and hammered iron.

items.title: Chipped Flint and Polished Stone

metrics.label: Raw Material
metrics.value: Hard flint nodules and tough quarry stones gathered from rivers and chalk.

metrics.label: How Makers Shaped It
metrics.value: Struck by flint knapping for sharp flakes or rubbed smooth on wet sandstone.

metrics.label: Strengths and Limits
metrics.value: Razor-sharp for meat and trees, but a snapped stone axe could never be melted down.

items.takeaway: Clever flint handaxes and polished stone axes helped hunters and first farmers survive long before metal arrived.

items.title: Cast Copper and Tin Bronze

metrics.label: Raw Material
metrics.value: Nine parts copper rock from Wales melted with one part tin ore from Cornwall.

metrics.label: How Makers Shaped It
metrics.value: Smelted over hot charcoal fires and poured as glowing liquid into two-piece stone moulds.

metrics.label: Strengths and Limits
metrics.value: Cleared woodland faster and broken blades could be remelted, though copper and tin were rare.

items.takeaway: Mixing copper and tin gave Bronze Age communities gleaming axes, shields, and swords that could be cast again.

items.title: Hammered Red-Hot Iron

metrics.label: Raw Material
metrics.value: Common reddish iron ore dug straight from British hills and bogs.

metrics.label: How Makers Shaped It
metrics.value: Heated in roaring clay furnaces until glowing hot, then hammered into shape by blacksmiths.

metrics.label: Strengths and Limits
metrics.value: Tougher than bronze and plentiful across Britain, making strong ploughshares that sliced heavy clay soil.

items.takeaway: Tough iron ploughshares helped Celtic farmers grow bumper wheat harvests that supported busy tribes and giant hillforts.
